name: Thoracic extension over foam roller

card.summary: A mobility drill that arches the upper back over a foam roller, used to counter rounded posture; no trials of the drill itself were found.
card.aka: Foam roller thoracic mobilization, upper back extension
card.note: Related literature covers thoracic manipulation and sitting posture, not this specific drill.

quick.overview:
The drill involves lying with a foam roller under the upper back and extending the thoracic spine over it. It is discussed in posture routines aimed at rounded upper back and forward head carriage.

No clinical study of the foam-roller drill was located. Related research examines thoracic manipulation for neck pain and the muscle activity in different sitting postures.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say it mobilizes stiff thoracic joints so the upper back can extend and the shoulders and head sit further back. This is a proposed mechanism not demonstrated by trials of the drill.
quick.risks: No harms are documented in the sources reviewed; people with spinal conditions are generally referred to clinicians for exercise advice.

lead: Thoracic extension over a foam roller is a self-mobilization exercise in which the upper back is arched back over a roller. It is used in posture-focused routines for stiffness and a flexed upper back.

Wikipedia describes forward head posture as associated with a hunched thoracic spine and lists thoracic mobilization among proposed remedies, citing a randomized trial in which thoracic manipulation reduced neck pain immediately; it also notes that some of its treatment claims need better sourcing [1]. That trial studied clinician-delivered manipulation, not foam-roller self-mobilization.

paras: No studies found. Related studies examined spinal-pelvic curvature and trunk muscle activation in different upright sitting postures in pain-free people [2], and neck pain sensorimotor tests [3]; neither tested a foam-roller drill.

refs.title: Effect of different upright sitting postures on spinal-pelvic curvature and trunk muscle activation in a pain-free population
